title: Relay chariots
hook: seven chariots in relay, each for one stage of the road

segments.voice: Yesterday: the anthill, and your line, dig carefully. Did you turn over one piece of your own anthill, slowly, without hacking at it? Day four hundred twenty-two.

Two monks have heard of each other and never met. One is Sariputta, the Buddha's chief disciple for wisdom. The other is Punna, son of Mantani, praised to the Buddha by the monks of his home country. Sariputta wants to meet him. So he follows Punna into a grove called the Blind Men's Wood, sits down under a tree a little way off, and when the afternoon is ending, walks over and starts asking questions. Punna has no idea who he's talking to. Today: relay chariots.
screen: `TWO MONKS WHO NEVER MET.` → `A GROVE, A TREE, AN AFTERNOON.` → `PUNNA DOESN'T KNOW WHO'S ASKING.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-fourth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. Sariputta asks: why do you live the holy life? For pure virtue? No. For a pure mind? No. For pure view? No. He goes down a list of seven purities, and Punna says no to every one. Then what for? For final release without clinging, Punna says. Then is final release the same as pure virtue? No. Is it something apart from all seven? Also no. So Punna gives a picture. King Pasenadi lives in Savatthi and has urgent business in Saketa, a long way off. So he sets out seven chariots in relay along the road. He rides the first to the second, climbs down, rides the second to the third, and so on, until the seventh brings him to the palace gate in Saketa. Now someone at the gate asks: did you come here from Savatthi in this chariot? If the king says yes, that's not quite true. The honest answer names the whole relay. Each chariot only had to reach the next one. That's how the seven purities work, Punna says. Pure virtue is for the sake of a pure mind. A pure mind is for the sake of pure view. And so on down the road, until the last purity carries you to release. None of them is the goal. Each is there for the sake of the next. Then the two men learn each other's names, and each praises the other. The picture works off the cushion too: on a long road, today's job is only to reach the next chariot.
screen: `WHY DO YOU LIVE THE HOLY LIFE?` · `SEVEN CHARIOTS FROM SAVATTHI TO SAKETA` · `EACH ONE ONLY REACHES THE NEXT` · `NONE IS THE GOAL; EACH SERVES THE NEXT` · then, large: `ONE STAGE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of something long you're in the middle of: a recovery, a degree, a hard year, a habit you're rebuilding. Don't picture the finish. Picture only the next chariot, the one small stretch that's actually in front of you this week. Then let the picture go and sit with the breath, one breath as one stage, then the next. When the mind runs ahead to the palace gate, bring it back to this chariot. The bell holds the time.
Relay chariots. Seven purities, each one there to carry you to the next, until the last brings you to release. Today's word.
Your line: one stage at a time. Today, when the whole road feels too long, name only the next chariot, and ride that one. Day four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, the seven purifications from this discourse later shaped Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, where a practitioner's progress is described stage by stage, each purity resting on the one before.

fork.setup: you're King Pasenadi, arriving at the palace gate in Saketa. someone asks: did this chariot bring you all the way from Savatthi? what's the honest answer?
options: no: seven chariots, each to the next.
no chariot brought me; I walked.
fork.reveal: Punna's point: the last chariot only covered the last stretch. the whole relay brought the king, the way seven purities carry someone to release.

original.note: Pali ratha: chariot. the discourse is called the Rathavinita Sutta, the relay of chariots.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a king's travel plans.
what it means: each stage of practice exists to carry you to the next one, and none of them is the goal by itself.
what a scholar hears: MN 24's seven purifications later became a guiding frame for Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 24, Rathavinita Sutta (the relay chariots)

notes: MN 24 paraphrased: meeting in Andhavana (Blind Men's Grove) near Savatthi; Sariputta sits under a tree for the day's abiding, approaches in the evening; Punna learns his name only at the end. Please confirm details.
The seven purities are named only generally (virtue, mind, view, and so on) to keep the teach simple.

Visuddhimagga's use of the seven purifications as its frame: confirm the description in howItsDone and the trapdoor. Reviewer softened the trapdoor from 'the whole structure' to 'a guiding frame': the Visuddhimagga is also organized as virtue, concentration and wisdom, with the later purifications mainly shaping the wisdom chapters. Fifth-century dating given as 'usually dated'.
